q: Since 2008, US prostate cancer incidence has been:
e: SEER data show a peak in 1992, about 5 years after PSA testing began, then a fall to 1995 and year-to-year fluctuation until 2008. Incidence has fallen steadily since then.

q: Globally, age-standardised prostate cancer incidence is highest in:
o: High-income regions where PSA testing is common
e: Incidence follows screening intensity. Incidence and mortality are highest in African American and Jamaican men.

q: The main criticism of the PLCO screening trial is:
o: Heavy PSA testing in the control arm (contamination about 52%) plus pre-screening
e: When analysed by actual screening received, PLCO's results resembled ERSPC's, showing a mortality benefit.

q: A man whose father had prostate cancer has a relative risk of about:
e: Risk rises with the number of affected relatives, how closely related they are, and how young they were at diagnosis. HOXB13 and BRCA2 carry substantially higher risk.

q: Which effect of obesity is described in prostate cancer?
o: Lower serum PSA (and larger glands), with more high-grade disease and worse outcomes after surgery
e: Lower PSA and larger prostates may delay biopsy and increase sampling error.

q: TMPRSS2-ERG fusion:
o: Places an ETS oncogene under androgen control; found in about 50% of localised cancers and highly specific for cancer
e: TMPRSS2 is an androgen-regulated, prostate-specific serine protease gene. When present, the fusion is close to 100% specific for prostate cancer.

q: SPOP-mutant tumours that overexpress SPINK1 are:
o: More common in African American men and associated with higher Gleason scores
e: SPOP mutations account for about 10% of primary cancers. Fusions and SPOP mutations are usually mutually exclusive.

q: Which statement on androgens and prostate cancer is correct?
o: Hypogonadal men never get prostate cancer
Higher serum testosterone clearly raises risk
Androgen exposure before or at puberty is needed for prostate cancer to develop
Type 1 5α-reductase is the main prostatic isoform
e: DHT made by type 2 5α-reductase is the main prostatic androgen. Intraprostatic androgen levels are locally regulated, and no dose–response with serum levels has been shown.

q: SELECT showed that:
o: Selenium plus vitamin E lowered prostate cancer
Vitamin E alone increased prostate cancer risk on longer follow-up (HR about 1.17)
e: Neither supplement prevented prostate cancer.

q: In PCPT (finasteride) and REDUCE (dutasteride), 5-ARIs:
o: Reduced the risk of being diagnosed with prostate cancer by about 25%, with no effect on overall or cancer-specific mortality
e: More high-grade cancers were diagnosed on 5-ARIs, but this did not increase deaths.

q: PSA is specific for:
o: The prostate as an organ, not any one disease
e: Its half-life is 2–3 days. PSA can be made outside the prostate, for example in breast, adrenal and renal tumours.

q: Compared with normal tissue, prostate cancer cells make:
o: Less PSA per gram; serum PSA rises because the tissue architecture breaks down
e: Cancer tissue has up to 1.5-fold lower PSA mRNA.

q: Men with prostate cancer have a ___ percentage of free PSA than men without cancer:
e: PSA from cancer cells escapes proteolytic processing, so more circulates bound to ACT (α1-antichymotrypsin). Percent free PSA is FDA-approved for men with a normal DRE and PSA 4–10 ng/mL.

q: After starting finasteride, total PSA ___ and percent free PSA ___:
e: Total and free PSA fall together, so the ratio stays about the same.

q: PCA3 is:
o: A prostate-specific non-coding RNA measured in urine
e: It lies on chromosome 9q21–22 and has no open reading frame. It can be combined with urinary TMPRSS2:ERG.

q: Compared with PSA, hK2 (human kallikrein 2) in cancer tissue is:
e: Benign epithelium expresses PSA strongly and hK2 weakly. hK2 is part of the 4Kscore.

q: proPSA ([−2]proPSA, used in the Prostate Health Index) is:
o: An inactive precursor that still carries part of its leader peptide, circulating as free PSA
e: hK2 removes the 7-amino-acid pro-leader to activate PSA. Truncated forms ([−2], [−4], [−5]) make up much of the free PSA in cancer.

q: Which marker, when present, is close to 100% specific for prostate cancer but only about 50% sensitive?
e: It is an early event in carcinogenesis.

q: Which genes are classically hypermethylated (silenced) in prostate cancer?
e: GSTP1 hypermethylation is the best known, and is used in tissue-based tests for repeat biopsy.

q: Match the tissue genomic test to its basis. Which is correct?
o: Prolaris: 31 cell-cycle progression genes; Oncotype DX Prostate: 12 genes in 4 pathways; Decipher: 22-marker genomic classifier
e: All work on small amounts of formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissue and add prognostic information beyond Gleason score. Inherited genes that predispose to aggressive disease include BRCA1/2 and ATM.

q: Corpora amylacea (prostatic calcifications) are most commonly seen:
o: Along the surgical capsule between the transition and peripheral zones
e: Small diffuse calcifications are an incidental finding of ageing. Larger symptomatic calculi may reflect infection.

q: The normal adult seminal vesicle on TRUS is:
o: About 4.5–5.5 cm long, 2 cm wide, saccular and symmetric
e: Cystic seminal vesicle masses are usually benign. A solid mass may be malignant or, in endemic regions, due to schistosomiasis.

q: Which statement about hypoechoic prostate lesions is correct?
o: They should be biopsied, but can also be granulomatous prostatitis, infarct, lymphoma or BPH nodules; 39% of cancers are isoechoic
e: About 1% of cancers are hyperechoic. Hypoechogenicity does not correlate with grade.

q: Increasing the frequency of the ultrasound probe:
o: Increases resolution but reduces penetration depth
e: Remove any air between the probe and the tissue. The needle path is best seen in the sagittal plane.

q: Periprostatic block for TRUS biopsy is typically given:
o: With lidocaine through a long 22-gauge needle via the probe's biopsy channel, near the neurovascular bundles at the base and seminal vesicle junction
e: About 5 mL each side. Intrarectal gel alone is less effective.

q: The minimum number of systematic cores recommended at initial biopsy is:
e: Going to 18–20 cores at first biopsy adds little. The chapter predates MRI-first pathways (PRECISION). Now, targeted cores are added to systematic ones.

q: Which is NOT a risk factor for infection after prostate biopsy?
e: Non-white race, comorbidities, diabetes, a large prostate, foreign travel and recent antibiotics raise the risk (fluoroquinolone resistance).

q: Which statement about prophylaxis for TRUS biopsy is correct?
o: Epididymitis is the most common infection
It reduces, but does not abolish, febrile UTI needing admission
e: The book recommends a fluoroquinolone. Current EAU guidance prefers the transperineal route and discourages fluoroquinolones because of resistance and EMA safety restrictions.

q: Haematospermia after prostate biopsy:
o: Can last 4–6 weeks and is harmless
e: Counsel patients beforehand. Other complications: febrile UTI, sepsis, rectal bleeding and retention.

q: After an initial negative biopsy, repeat biopsies:
o: Find progressively fewer cancers (about 22% first biopsy, then 10%, 5%, 4%), which tend to be lower grade and stage
e: If cancer is suspected after several negative biopsies, the anterior zone and apex are the likeliest sites, best reached by template or fusion biopsy.

q: Four of 12 cores show only seminal vesicle in a 52-year-old Black man whose father died of prostate cancer (PSA 3). Next step:
o: Repeat a properly directed systematic biopsy
e: One seminal vesicle core is not unusual, but four means the biopsy was poorly directed in a high-risk man.

q: High-grade PIN (prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia):
o: If it is in only one core, it does not need repeat biopsy; it does not raise PSA
Is the same as intraductal carcinoma
e: Intraductal carcinoma is worse, goes with high-grade invasive cancer, and is treated as such. Low-grade PIN carries no extra risk.

q: Gleason grading is based on:
e: On needle biopsy, add the most common pattern and the highest pattern. At prostatectomy, add the most common and second most common, and report any tertiary pattern.

q: Gleason 4+4=8 is grade group:
e: GG1 ≤6; GG2 3+4; GG3 4+3; GG4 8; GG5 9–10. This grouping best separates prognosis.

q: Which finding at radical prostatectomy has NO independent prognostic value?
e: Perineural invasion is how cancer leaves the gland, but in the prostatectomy specimen it does not worsen prognosis. Vascular invasion does.

q: Which statement about tumour location is correct?
o: Tumour volume is an independent predictor after grade, stage and margins
Most are in the transition zone
Transition-zone tumours spread out of the gland at smaller volumes
About 85% are in the peripheral zone and about 85% are multifocal; even T1c tumours are mostly posterior/posterolateral
e: Transition-zone tumours need larger volumes before they extend out of the gland.

q: What distinguishes benign from malignant prostate glands on immunostaining?
o: Basal cells, shown by high-molecular-weight cytokeratin and p63, are present in benign glands and absent in cancer
e: A biopsy with a basal layer is benign. With an abnormal DRE, follow PSA and DRE closely.

q: pT2x on a radical prostatectomy report means:
o: The tumour is organ-confined except at a positive margin from an intraprostatic incision, where extension cannot be judged
e: Subdividing pT2 adds nothing to prognosis. Seminal vesicle invasion (pT3b) is almost always by direct spread.

q: Adenosis (atypical adenomatous hyperplasia):
o: Is found in the transition zone, can mimic cancer, and carries no added cancer risk
e: Note the difference from ASAP (atypical small acinar proliferation), which carries a high chance of cancer on rebiopsy.

q: Prostate cancer most commonly spreads, in order, to:
o: Lymph nodes, bone, lung, bladder, liver, adrenal
e: Only about 25% of men with seminal vesicle invasion, and few with nodal disease, are free of biochemical recurrence 10 years after prostatectomy.

q: Most immunodetectable serum PSA (65–90%) is bound to:
e: Complexes with α1-protease inhibitor (API) also exist. α2-macroglobulin-bound PSA is not detected by standard assays.

q: A man has a raised PSA with no symptoms. The AUA-supported next step is:
o: Repeat the PSA after a period of observation
e: Empirical antibiotics are not recommended. Ejaculation can raise PSA for up to 24 hours. DRE does not change it meaningfully.

q: A 60-year-old on finasteride for 7 years has a PSA of 4 ng/mL. His approximate untreated equivalent is:
e: Correction factors: double after 12 months, ×2.3 at 2 years, ×2.5 at 7 years. A rising PSA on a 5-ARI should raise suspicion of cancer.

q: Which lowers serum PSA?
e: BPH, prostatitis, manipulation and cancer raise it. African American men have higher PSA values.

q: In men with PSA 4–10, a PSA velocity above ___ ng/mL/year raises concern for cancer:
e: A free PSA above 25% is reassuring. A baseline PSA below 1 ng/mL at age 40–45 may justify less frequent testing.

q: Which single test has the highest positive predictive value for prostate cancer?
e: Pelvic lymphadenectomy remains the gold standard for nodal staging, because imaging misses micrometastases.

q: With PSA 4–10 ng/mL, roughly what proportion of cancers are organ-confined?
e: About 80% are organ-confined when PSA is under 4. More than half have disease beyond the prostate when PSA is over 10. About 20% have positive nodes when PSA is over 20, and about 75% when it is over 50.

q: The Partin tables predict pathological stage from:
o: Clinical stage, serum PSA and Gleason score
e: The chapter's bone scan rule (only if PSA >20, T3/T4 or bone symptoms) predates PSMA PET, which has largely replaced conventional imaging for high-risk staging.

q: Which finding at radical prostatectomy most strongly predicts hidden distant disease?
o: Seminal vesicle invasion or lymph node metastases
e: Only about 50% of men with positive margins progress.

q: A man with a previous negative 12-core biopsy has a stable PSA, but MRI shows a left peripheral-zone lesion that is dark on T2, restricts diffusion and shows early contrast enhancement and washout. Next step:
e: Agreement across T2, DWI and DCE sequences strongly suggests cancer. Fusion biopsy needs software registration of MRI to real-time TRUS.
